Injunctions under Nepalese Civil Procedure: Protecting Your Rights During Trial

📅 Published: 2025-02-10
🔄 Updated: 2025-10-01
⏱ 8 min read
🔍 Review: Senior Advocate Lead Counsel, Supreme Court Bar Association
Direct Legal Answer & Overview

An injunction under Chapter 13 of the Muluki Civil Procedure Code 2074 is a judicial order commanding an opposing party to do or refrain from doing a specific act. The court grants an interim injunction (Antarim Aadesh) prior to final judgment upon satisfying three cumulative legal tests: 1) A prima facie case showing a legitimate legal right; 2) The threat of irreparable injury (Apranipurna Kshati) that cannot be adequately cured by monetary damages; and 3) The balance of convenience (Subidha ko Asantulan) favoring the applicant.

Key Practical Takeaways

  • Interim orders (Antarim Aadesh) preserve the status quo to prevent destruction or sale of property during litigation.
  • Courts apply the three-prong test: Prima facie case, irreparable harm, and balance of convenience.
  • Violating a court injunction constitutes contempt of court punishable by fine or detention.

When a commercial partner threatens to liquidate disputed collateral, or a neighbor begins constructing a wall encroaching upon your land, waiting one to two years for a final court trial offers little comfort. In such urgent situations, Nepalese civil jurisprudence provides a vital emergency remedy: Court Injunctions (निषेधाज्ञा / अन्तरिम आदेश).

1. Types of Injunctions under Chapter 13 of the Civil Procedure Code

The Muluki Civil Procedure Code 2074 categorizes injunctive relief into three distinct forms:

  • Temporary / Interim Injunction (अन्तरिम आदेश): An emergency interlocutory order issued during ongoing litigation to maintain the status quo until the lawsuit concludes.
  • Prohibitory Injunction (निषेधाज्ञा): A permanent decree awarded at the conclusion of trial forbidding the defendant from repeating an unlawful infringement.
  • Mandatory Injunction (सकारात्मक आदेश): An affirmative order directing a party to take a positive step, such as demolishing an encroaching structure or restoring an obstructed easement.

2. The Three Cumulative Tests Applied by Nepalese Judges

Securing an interim injunction requires satisfying the court on three well-established legal principles:

  1. Prima Facie Case: The applicant must produce credible documents showing a bona fide legal right that requires judicial protection.
  2. Irreparable Injury (अपूरणीय क्षति): The applicant must demonstrate that if the injunction is refused, they will suffer substantial injury that cannot be remedied by future monetary compensation.
  3. Balance of Convenience (सुविधाको असन्तुलन): The court weighs whether the hardship caused to the applicant by refusing the order exceeds the inconvenience caused to the defendant by granting it.

3. Enforcement & Penalties for Disobedience

A court injunction order is legally binding from the instant it is pronounced. If an opposing party willfully violates an injunction, the aggrieved party can initiate contempt proceedings under the Administration of Justice Act 2073, which empowers the court to impose fines or order custodial detention of the violator.

Statutory Citations & Governing Nepal Legislation

Statute / Act Section / Rule Legal Significance
Muluki Civil Procedure Code 2074 Chapter 13 (Provisions relating to Injunction) Sections 154 to 160 governing grant of interim and permanent prohibitory orders.
Administration of Justice Act 2073 Section 17 (Contempt Powers) Penalties for disobeying lawful court injunction orders.

Documentary Checklist for this Procedure

  • ✔ Urgent petition for interim injunction supported by affidavit (Shapathpatra)
  • ✔ Photographic or documentary proof of immediate threat (demolition notice, construction photos)
  • ✔ Underlying title deed or contract evidencing prima facie legal right

Frequently Asked Questions on this Topic

Can an interim injunction be granted without hearing the other party (Ex-Parte)?

Under urgent circumstances where immediate irreversible harm would occur before summons can be served, Section 156 allows the judge to grant a short-term temporary interim order ex-parte, while summoning the opposing party for a bilateral hearing within 7 to 15 days.
